answers: Master data covers: chart of accounts, companies (us, customers, suppliers), catalogue service items, and VAT rates — each as a separate master-data object; companies also store an IBAN where available.

So when we talk about master data, we're looking at four things that each get their own master-data object: the chart of accounts, all the companies we work with — that means ourselves, our customers, and our suppliers — the services we offer listed as catalogue items, and the VAT rates; and on top of that, every company record also holds a bank account number in IBAN format whenever we actually have that information.
Chart of accounts, companies (our own outfit, customers, suppliers), catalogue service items, VAT rates — each one's its own master-data object; company records also carry the IBAN when we've got it.

Sales invoices we issue are recorded as sales_invoice documents. Each one carries: number, issue date, seller and buyer (looked up by NIP), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + payment days shown on the invoice; status begins as open, may later become paid. Open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched — a partly paid invoice remains open. Every sales invoice posts to book pl-stat: debit 201 for the gross, credit 701 for the net, credit 222 for the VAT.

So whenever we send out a sales invoice, the system creates a document of type sales_invoice, and that document holds all of the following: the invoice number, the issue date, the seller and the buyer — both identified by NIP — the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code pulled straight from the invoice. From those, the system calculates VAT as the net amount multiplied by the rate's percentage and then divided by 100, with the result rounded half up to the nearest grosz; the gross is simply net plus that VAT; the due date is worked out by adding the payment days that are printed on the invoice to the issue date; and the status is set to open right from the start, though it can move to paid later on. The open amount begins life equal to the gross and then gets reduced whenever payments are matched against the invoice — if it's only partly paid, the invoice stays open rather than flipping to paid. And on the bookkeeping side, every single sales invoice gets posted into book pl-stat with three lines: a debit to account 201 for the gross amount, a credit to account 701 for the net amount, and a credit to account 222 for the VAT amount.

Each invoice we put out? That's a sales_invoice document — got your number, issue date, seller and buyer by NIP, net amount, currency, VAT rate code, the whole lot. VAT gets calc'd as net times the rate percent over 100, half-up rounding to the grosz; gross is just net plus VAT; due date is issue date plus however many payment days the invoice says; status kicks off as open and can flip to paid down the line. Open amount starts at gross and drops as payments get matched — partly paid still means open. Posting goes into pl-stat: debit 201 at gross, credit 701 at net, credit 222 at VAT.

A supplier's invoice turns into a purchase_invoice document with these fields: number, invoice date, supplier looked up by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate percent ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT. Status begins as open and shifts to paid once settled. The open amount starts equal to the gross and falls as payments are matched; partial payment leaves the status open. Posting goes to book pl-stat: debit 402 for the net, debit 221 for the VAT, credit 202 for the gross.

So when a supplier sends us an invoice, what we do is create a document of type purchase_invoice, and on that document we record the number, the invoice date, the supplier — we find them using their NIP — our own company as the owner, the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. Then the VAT figure is worked out by taking the net, multiplying it by the rate's percent, dividing by 100, and rounding half up to the nearest grosz, and the gross is simply the net plus that VAT. The document's status kicks off as open and can eventually move over to paid. The open amount starts out matching the gross and gets reduced each time a payment is matched against it, but if only some payments have come in the status stays open. For the bookkeeping side, every purchase invoice gets posted in book pl-stat: we debit account 402 with the net, debit account 221 with the VAT, and credit account 202 with the gross.

Basically, a supplier invoice comes in and we slap it into the system as a purchase_invoice — it's got the number, invoice date, the supplier pulled up by NIP, our company as the owner, the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. VAT gets calc'd as net times the rate percent over 100, rounded half up to the grosz, and gross is just net plus VAT. It kicks off with status open and eventually flips to paid. The open amount starts at the gross and chips down as payments get matched; if it's only partly paid, it stays open. Book pl-stat gets the posting: debit 402 for the net, debit 221 for the VAT, credit 202 for the gross.

Each line on a bank statement generates a bank_line record carrying: date, amount, currency, direction, the line's title as reference, the counterparty and its account, and our account; the open amount is initialised to the full amount, and the status begins as open, flipping to settled once the open amount reaches zero. Incoming money is applied to the open sales invoices of the customer identified by the source account, working through this priority sequence: the invoice explicitly named in the title; that same named invoice when the payment is within 0.02 short or over and the gap is written off to account 755; an invoice whose total matches exactly; the smallest combination of invoices, capped at 4, whose totals sum to the amount; the named invoice covered partially; and finally, starting from the oldest, whichever open invoices the money will reach. Outgoing money follows the identical sequence against the open purchase invoices of the supplier identified by the destination account, but without the 0.02 tolerance rule. Each match reduces the open amounts on both the affected invoices and the bank line by the allocated figure, marking each as paid or settled when nothing remains open, and logs one settlement record per invoice containing the payment, the document type and id, the amount, and the date. Any tolerated difference produces a matching difference record holding: kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date; when the difference is short, it is additionally posted in book pl-stat as a debit to the difference account and a credit to account 201.

So what happens is, every single line that comes in on a bank statement gets turned into its own bank_line record — that record stores the date, the amount, the currency, the direction, the title of the line as its reference, who the counterparty is and what their account number is, plus our own account; the open amount on that record kicks off equal to the full amount, and the status starts out as open and then switches over to settled once there's nothing left open on it. Now, when money is coming in, the system goes and looks at the open sales invoices belonging to whichever customer owns the account the money came from, and it tries to match in a very specific order: first it looks for the invoice that's actually named in the title; then, if that named invoice is off by no more than 0.02 — either short or over — it still matches it and writes the difference off to account 755; after that it hunts for any invoice that's for exactly that amount; then it tries to find the fewest invoices it can combine, with a hard limit of 4, that add up to the total; next it partially covers the named invoice if nothing else has worked; and as a last resort it just pays off the oldest open invoices in order until the money runs out. Money going out follows that exact same sequence but against the open purchase invoices of whichever supplier the money is heading to, and the 0.02 tolerance thing doesn't apply there. Whenever a match happens, the open amounts on the invoices involved and on the bank line itself drop by however much was allocated — they get marked paid, or settled if they're fully cleared — and the system writes a settlement record for each invoice that got touched, capturing the payment, the document type and id, the amount, and the date. If there's a tolerated difference, a matching difference record gets created for it with the kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date all stored on it; and specifically when the difference is short, a posting also goes into book pl-stat, debiting the difference account and crediting account 201.

Bank statement line → bank_line record. Fields: date, amount, currency, direction, title-as-reference, counterparty + counterparty account, our account. Open amount initialises to the amount; status is open, becomes settled when open amount hits zero. For money in, match against the source customer's open sales invoices in strict order: (1) the invoice named in the title; (2) that named invoice when the gap is at most 0.02 short or over, writing the difference to 755; (3) an invoice for exactly that amount; (4) the fewest invoices summing to it, max 4; (5) the named invoice partially; (6) oldest open invoices until funds run out. Money out: same sequence against the destination supplier's open purchase invoices, no tolerance. On a match, open amounts on the invoices and the line decrease by the allocated figure — paid or settled when zero remains — and one settlement record is written per invoice: payment, document type and id, amount, date. A tolerated difference produces a matching difference record: kind, amount, currency, direction, account, date. A short difference is also posted in book pl-stat: debit the difference account, credit 201.

Complaints get logged as complaint docs with a number, customer, and details fields. Each one automatically spins up a linked case-type record where the subject equals the complaint number and the status is open, moving to resolved later.

So basically when a complaint comes in, you slap it into a complaint document — you've got your number, your customer, your details — and that kicks off a follow-up thing, which is a new type called case, and its subject is set to the complaint number, it starts off as open, and down the line it can flip to resolved.

Each complaint is recorded in a complaint document carrying a number, a customer, and details. Upon registration, a corresponding record of type case is created, with its subject set to the complaint number, its initial status set to open, and a later possible transition to resolved.
A withdrawn complaint gets its case closed as resolved.
So basically, if the customer decides to pull back their complaint, what happens is that the case tied to it ends up being marked as resolved.
Customer pulls the complaint? Case goes resolved.
